passage: Saturday. Today Akash's face was red when I found him near the gate. Three boys from the next lane were laughing at his stammer and calling him names. My hands went cold. I wanted to shout, but I walked over, stood beside him and said, "That is my cousin. Please stop." My voice shook, but it came out calm. One boy smirked and they walked off, still muttering. Akash held my sleeve all the way home and whispered, "Thank you, didi." I told Chachi what happened, just in case they come back. I did not need to hit anyone, and I am glad. Aparna.

qa.a: She found Akash near the gate.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling as she walked over to the boys?
qa.a: She was scared and angry: her hands went cold and she wanted to shout, but she stayed calm.

qa.q: Why did telling Chachi help, even though the boys had left?
qa.a: Telling an adult means someone else knows and can step in if the teasing returns, so Aparna and Akash are not alone with it.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Aparna stood beside him?
qa.a: Akash probably felt protected and relieved, which is shown by how he held her sleeve all the way home. 🤍

grounding: A child steps in calmly beside her small cousin who is being teased, then tells an adult; fighting was not needed.

passage: Last Diwali holidays my small cousin Kunal came to stay with us in Indore. He is six and has a stammer. On the second evening, three boys from the next building copied him outside the gate: 'K-k-k-Kunal!' He froze with his sparkler box, face crumpling. My blood went hot. I'm Ganga, and part of me wanted to shove the biggest boy into the drain. Instead I walked over and stood right beside Kunal, my hand on his shoulder. 'He's my cousin. Stop it,' I said, as steadily as I could. One boy laughed and started again. So I said, 'Fine, I'm calling my uncle,' and shouted for Chacha from the gate. Chacha came down at once, and the boys left. Kunal held my hand all evening.

qa.q: What was Kunal holding when the boys teased him?
What did Ganga feel when the boys copied Kunal?
qa.a: Angry and protective; Ganga's blood went hot, and part of Ganga wanted to shove the biggest boy.

qa.q: Which steps did Ganga take instead of fighting?
qa.a: Standing beside Kunal, speaking steadily, and calling Chacha when the teasing continued.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt with Ganga beside him?
qa.a: Safer and less alone; he held Ganga's hand all evening.

grounding: A child protects a small cousin from teasing by standing beside him, speaking calmly and fetching an adult.

passage:
Note from Himani Joshi, tuition teacher, to Hemant's parents.
From my balcony this evening I saw something you should know about. Some older boys in the park were grabbing your nephew Bittu's cap and tossing it over his head while he jumped for it, crying. Hemant ran over from the swings. He didn't shout or push. He stood in front of Bittu and said, 'Give it back. He's four.' His voice was shaking a little, but he kept looking at the tallest boy. When they kept tossing it, Hemant took Bittu's hand and walked straight to the guard's cabin. The guard got the cap back and sent the boys off. Hemant chose calm over a fight. I thought you would want to know.

qa.q: Where did Hemant take Bittu when the boys kept tossing the cap?
What does Hemant's shaking voice suggest?
qa.a: He was nervous and scared of the older boys, but protective enough to keep standing in front of Bittu.

qa.q: Why was going to the guard a wise step?
qa.a: The teasing kept going, so fetching an adult solved it without a fight.

qa.q: What was it like for Bittu when the boys took his cap?
qa.a: Frightening and upsetting; he was crying and jumping for it, so Hemant's help probably felt like a rescue.

grounding: A tuition teacher's note describes a boy protecting his small cousin from older boys calmly and fetching an adult.
